anchor: WHo ever comes to shroud me
title: Opening and occasion
short: The dead lover speaks to whoever will wrap his corpse, forbidding them to touch the bracelet of hair on his arm.
body: The poem is spoken from beyond death: 'shroud' means to wrap a corpse in a winding-sheet. It was printed in 1633 and belongs to a group of poems (with 'The Blossome', 'The Primrose' and 'The Relique') that recur together in the manuscripts. Grierson thought it probable that this sequence was addressed to Magdalen Herbert, mother of George Herbert, in the earlier days of Donne's acquaintance with her; there is no firm evidence. The lady of this poem is the conventional Petrarchan mistress whose cruelty has killed her lover, whereas in 'The Relique' Grierson hears a Platonic tone.

title: That subtile wreath of haire
greek: Latin subtilis (finely woven, from sub + tela, web)
short: A bracelet of the lady's hair, a common love-token, worn round the dead man's arm.
body: 'Subtile' means fine, delicate, finely woven, with a hint of 'cunning' that the poem will develop. Bracelets of a beloved's hair were real tokens of the period. Grierson illustrates the custom from Sir Kenelm Digby's Private Memoirs, in which Theagenes (Digby himself) wears a bracelet of Stelliana's hair about his arm, later throwing it into the fire when he heard that she was to marry another. The same token returns in Donne's 'The Relique': 'A bracelet of bright haire about the bone'.

title: crowne, my arme
short: The text here has a comma after 'crowne'; Grierson prints 'crowns my arme': the hair encircles the arm as a crown does a head.
body: Grierson's text reads 'which crowns my arme', and modern editions agree; the comma here is probably a punctuation slip, and the sense is 'which crowns my arm'. The verb is a deliberate hyperbole: a crown belongs on the head, the seat of the soul and of government, and this wreath will indeed claim to govern the body as the soul's 'Viceroy'. The word thus opens the political conceit of the first stanza.

title: The mystery, the signe
short: Religious terms: the hair is a sacred mystery and an outward sign, like a sacrament, not to be handled.
body: 'Mystery' was the term for a sacrament (Latin sacramentum translates Greek mysterion), and the Book of Common Prayer's catechism defines a sacrament as an 'outward and visible sign' of an inward grace. The bracelet is such a sign of an inward reality, the lady's soul or love. The vocabulary begins the poem's play with sacred objects, which ends in 'martyr', 'idolatrie' and 'reliques'.

title: my outward Soule
short: Since his own soul has gone to heaven, the hair acts as an external soul, keeping the body from decay.
body: In scholastic thought the soul is the form that holds the body together; when it departs, the body dissolves. The speaker's real soul has gone 'unto heaven', so the hair, an 'outward Soule', is left to rule in its place. Donne's wit lies in taking a love-token literally as a metaphysical principle. The second stanza supplies a physiological reason for the claim.

title: Viceroy ... her Provinces
short: The hair is the soul's viceroy, governing the limbs as provinces of a kingdom while the king is absent.
body: A viceroy governs a province in the name of an absent sovereign, as Spanish viceroys ruled Naples or Peru. The soul, gone to heaven, leaves the hair to 'controule' the body; the limbs are 'her Provinces' (the soul's, grammatically feminine, as in Latin anima). The task is to keep them 'from dissolution', from both decay and political break-up. The political conceit of the body as a state was a commonplace that Donne sharpens by placing it in a corpse.

anchor: sinewie thread my braine lets fall
title: the sinewie thread
short: The nerves, thought to descend from the brain like threads, bind the body together; her hair should do it better.
body: Endicott glosses the 'sinewie thread' as the nervous system. Galenic anatomy described the nerves as issuing from the brain and spinal marrow and spreading through all parts, carrying the animal spirits that give sense and motion; in this sense they 'tye those parts' into one person. The lady's hairs grew 'upward' from 'a better braine' (hers), so they should be stronger ties still. The pseudo-scientific argument is typical of the Songs and Sonnets.

sources.cite: N. J. Endicott, notes to 'The Funeral', Representative Poetry Online (University of Toronto), l. 9

title: strength and art / Have from a better braine
short: Her hair draws strength and skill from her brain, which is better than his.
body: The compliment rests on the idea that hair grows from the brain, nourished by it. Hairs that 'upward grew' (on her head) are nearer heaven, and their 'art' may also hint at craft or cunning, recalling 'subtile' in l. 3. The stanza then swerves into suspicion: perhaps she meant the bracelet not as a soul but as a fetter. The hairs are thus a superior nervous system.

title: As prisoners then are manacled
short: Perhaps she gave the bracelet as a manacle, the fetters put on prisoners once they are condemned to death.
body: The 'except' clause reverses the stanza's flattering argument: the wreath might be a sign of his doom, like the irons placed on a prisoner condemned to execution. The long last line, with its stumbling elisions ('when they'are condem'nd'), imitates the weight of the chain. The ambiguity of the lady's intention is left open, and the next stanza begins by brushing it aside: 'What ere shee meant by'it'.

title: Loves martyr
short: Having died of the lady's cruelty, he is a martyr of love, and the hair would therefore become a relic.
body: The lover who dies for love as a martyr dies for faith is a Petrarchan commonplace, which Donne develops through Catholic devotional practice: martyrs' remains were venerated as relics. The same religious wit structures 'The Canonization' and 'The Relique'. The pathos of the dead lover is undercut by the playful precision with which he follows the logic of his metaphor.

title: it might breed idolatrie
short: In Protestant polemic, the veneration of relics was idolatry; burying the hair prevents a cult growing up.
body: Reformed critics of Rome attacked the veneration of saints' relics as idolatry, and the English Church had suppressed shrines and relic-cults. The dead speaker, prudently Protestant, asks for the hair to be buried with him lest others worship it. The joke depends on the reader's awareness of the controversy, in which Donne, born a Catholic and later an Anglican controversialist, was personally involved. 'The Relique' imagines exactly what this poem forbids: the bones and bracelet dug up and taken for relics.

title: reliques
short: Relics: the remains or belongings of a saint, kept and honoured after death.
body: From Latin reliquiae, remains. The word links the poem with 'The Relique', where the grave-digger finds 'A bracelet of bright haire about the bone' and the lovers become objects of misguided worship. Grierson notes that the two poems travel together in the manuscripts but differ in tone: here the lady is cruel and the love Petrarchan, there the relation has become Platonic.

title: humility ... bravery
short: It was humble to treat the hair as a soul; it is a splendid gesture of defiance to bury part of her.
body: Endicott glosses 'bravery' as 'a splendid gesture'; the word also carried the senses of bravado and of showy finery. The antithesis balances two attitudes in the lover: humility in honouring her token as if it could do 'all that a Soule can doe', and pride, or revenge, in taking part of her into the grave. The final stanza thus turns the poem from devotion to a sharp retort.

title: since you would have none of mee
short: The printed texts read 'have none of mee' (would not accept me); some manuscripts read 'save none of mee'. Grierson preferred 'save'.
body: 'Would have none of' means 'would not accept', a common idiom (Grierson cites Twelfth Night, 'she'll none of me'). Grierson found 'save' in the manuscript H49, and possibly in D, and adopted it, arguing that it was hard to see how it could arise as a corruption, that it gives a sharper antithesis (she would not save him, keep him alive, so he buries part of her), and that being saved is the lover's usual prayer. Many editors keep the 1633 reading, as this text does. Either way the final line's paradox stands: rejected whole, he takes a part of her to the grave.

title: Stanza form
short: Three eight-line stanzas of irregular line lengths, each ending in a long line that lets the argument settle.
body: Each stanza rhymes ababcdcd, with lines ranging from two or three stresses ('Nor question much', 'Through every part', 'For since I am') to long final lines of twelve syllables or more ('And keepe these limbes, her Provinces, from dissolution'). The short lines act as hesitations within the argument, while the drawn-out last line of each stanza gives a weight like a sentence passed. The pattern is repeated exactly in each stanza.
